title: Amazon app warns New York of higher costs if Mamdani delivery law passes
description: An Amazon driver loads packages into a delivery van at an Amazon delivery station in Alpharetta, Georgia, Nov. 28, 2022.Justin Sullivan | Getty Images
body: An Amazon driver loads packages into a delivery van at an Amazon delivery station in Alpharetta, Georgia, Nov. 28, 2022.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesAmazon is taking its fight against a New York City delivery bill, which has been backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, to its shopping website and app. Some users who open the company's shopping app or website report being served with pop-ups and banners warning that the New York City Council "could add up to $5 per order" if it passes Intro 518, or the Delivery Protection Act. The bill would require Amazon to employ its army of third-party delivery companies directly, disrupting the contractor model it has relied on since 2018. Amazon uses a network of thousands of small companies, which often work solely for Amazon, to handle the last-mile portion of shipments, in an effort to speed up deliveries and control more of its logistics operations. "If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city," Amazon's in-app message states. "That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees."The proposed legislation was introduced in February and is awaiting review by City Council Speaker Julie Menin.Amazon also posted a statement on its company website where it often publishes its policy positions. But rarely has the company used its valuable e-commerce site and app real estate to push its perspectives. Other tech companies including Uber and Lyft have similarly used their apps to advocate for or against legislation in the past. Amazon's pop-up notices and a stationary banner on its store homepage direct users to a form where they can "contact your council member to oppose Intro 518." According to Amazon, 20,000 customers sent emails to city council members in the first six hours that the pop-up appeared.Menin told CNBC in a statement that Amazon's claim it will need to raise prices due to the proposed legislation "defies logic." "We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs," Menin said. "If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong." Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement that the company put up the notices to be "transparent with our customers" about what the bill "would cause them if it passes as written." "If customers are concerned, one of the most impactful things they can do is contact their City Council member and ask them to oppose this bill," Nantel said. The Delivery Protection Act has received a swell of support from labor groups, including the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which has sought to unionize Amazon delivery and warehouse workers. Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon's subcontractor model "leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets." He's argued the bill would lead to safer working conditions for drivers, and allow the city to "regulate last-mile operations." Amazon disputed Mamdani's claims, saying the bill would put Delivery Service Partner jobs "at risk without improving safety." It also argued that other businesses and governments use contractors in their operations, and said the DSP model has allowed it to meet growing customer demand."It works because local entrepreneurs — people rooted in their communities — deliver a better experience," Amazon said. "They invest in their teams, their routes, and their neighborhoods. That's not a liability play." Amazon has lobbied heavily against the bill, while logistics and business groups have launched local advertising campaigns, and warned they may sue the city if the bill passes.

schema.headline: Amazon app warns New York of higher costs if Mamdani delivery law passes

title: 3-step method to influence people and win them over, from a Stanford expert: ‘Your voice is like a muscle’
description: Think back on the most memorable, inspiring speeches or presentations you've witnessed. They probably weren't delivered in a monotone, Matt Abrahams s
body: Think back on the most memorable, inspiring speeches or presentations you've witnessed. They probably weren't delivered in a monotone, Matt Abrahams says."The human brain is designed to pick out and focus on things that are novel and new," says Abrahams, a Stanford University lecturer on strategic communication and host of the "Think Fast, Talk Smart" podcast. "So anything that stays the same, like a monotonous voice or cadence, we don't pay as much attention to."Indeed, successful leaders often have an uncanny ability to win over a crowd: The power of persuasion lies not just in what you actually have to say, but also in how you say it, research shows. The topic has taken on new relevance this week as Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress steps into one of the most closely watched leadership roles in corporate America.In appearances this week, including Nvidia's quarterly earnings call and an interview with CNBC's "Mad Money" host Jim Cramer, Kress has discussed the company's performance. She's also addressed employees and investors in a time of leadership upheaval, following Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's high-profile resignation on Nov. 12.How Kress communicates has drawn attention and, in some circles, criticism. On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal described her public speaking style as "slow, steady, almost monotone." That doesn't necessarily make it ineffective. Her situation, however, highlights a broader challenge leaders face when they need to inform, reassure and persuade large groups of people at once.Generally speaking, anyone can stand a better chance at persuading others to follow them by honing an engaging speaking style, says Abrahams. Some people may be naturally expressive and engaging. For others, it's a skill that requires time and practice.Abrahams suggests a three-step playbook for anyone learning to speak more persuasively: "repetition, reflection and feedback."3 steps to influence people with your voice: 'Repetition, reflection and feedback'Abrahams' simplest advice for making yourself a more engaging speaker: "When you're using emotive words, reflect the emotion in them." That means adding some emphasis to words like "exciting," "huge" or "challenging," and so on. If you tend to speak monotonously, leaning into obviously emotive words can help you vary your tone and inflection enough to keep your audience's attention.There's a catch, of course: People find inauthenticity off-putting and disingenuous, says Abrahams. Don't alter your voice entirely, he suggests — just add some variety to your intonation and speaking volume. Learning to do so while still sounding natural takes practice, he notes."Your voice is like a muscle," says Abrahams. "You can train it. You can grow it [and] strengthen it, just like you go to the gym to lift weights."Practicing repetition starts with reading aloud from a chosen text, which Abrahams recommends so you don't have to overthink what you're saying. And the same way you might lift heavy weights to get stronger, Abrahams suggests reading overly expressive material to start getting out of your comfort zone and practice being energetic and engaging. He instructs his Stanford students to try reading Dr. Seuss books, as their playful words and bouncy rhymes can naturally make for a lively performance. While practicing reading out loud, record yourself to watch and listen to later, Abrahams recommends. Then, use the recording to reflect on what works and what doesn't, and incorporate your self-feedback into your next reading. You can also play the recording for a few trusted peers to get their thoughts, Abrahams says.If a line reading doesn't sound natural in your voice, feels flat or even rushed, keep trying it until you're satisfied, he says. Leaders are often asked to deliver lengthy speeches or talk for long periods in interviews and panels, so it's important to build your vocal stamina, he adds."We have to calibrate ourselves," he says.Abrahams asks his Stanford graduate students to review their recordings in three ways, he says:With no sound, so they can focus on their physical presenceWith sound only, so they can dissect their vocal deliveryAll together, to review the full performance"That's how you train your brain to see: 'What do I need to sound like?'" says Abrahams.

schema.headline: 3-step method to influence people and win them over, from a Stanford expert: ‘Your voice is like a muscle’

title: Kraken parent's acquisition of Tribe Capital flags new chapter in evolution of crypto exchanges
description: Timon Schneider | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesPayward, the owner of crypto exchange Kraken, is pushing into private markets with its latest acquisition,
body: Timon Schneider | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesPayward, the owner of crypto exchange Kraken, is pushing into private markets with its latest acquisition, underscoring a broader shift in cryptocurrencies, from trading-led growth to the buildout of financial infrastructure.Payward said late Wednesday that it's buying venture capital and asset management provider Tribe Capital Management, led by Payward's co-CEO Arjun Sethi. No purchase price was disclosed.Tribe, where Sethi is co-founder and chairman, invests across early- and late-stage private companies and has $2.7 billion in assets under management. "Joining Payward gives us the opportunity to bring Tribe's investment approach to a global financial platform," Jonathan Hsu, another co-founder of Tribe Capital, said in a statement. "We see a strong fit between our investment approach and Payward's infrastructure, distribution, and product-building capabilities."Payward didn't respond to a request for comment. The acquisition is novel among crypto exchanges. Unlike exchange-owned venture arms such as Coinbase Ventures or Binance Labs, Payward is looking to integrate Tribe's investment and fund-management capabilities into an existing custody, trading, collateral and tokenization infrastructure to develop private-market investment products. Payward is trying to position itself to capture value from a broader crypto-driven transformation of financial services, not use the venture vehicle to draw more capital into the crypto ecosystem. The acquisition is another step in the evolution in the crypto exchange business model. With cryptocurrency prices continuing to decline this year, crypto exchanges have worked to move past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, focusing instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance.watch now

schema.headline: Kraken parent's acquisition of Tribe Capital flags new chapter in evolution of crypto exchanges

title: Denmark ratifies Trump security deal over Greenland after months of diplomatic tensions
description: Denmark's Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen (sitting, R) attends the second legislative process and vote on the security agreement between Denmark
body: Denmark's Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen (sitting, R) attends the second legislative process and vote on the security agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the US in the Parliament Hall at Christiansborg in Copenhagen, on November 19, 2026.Mads Claus Rasmussen | Afp | Getty ImagesDanish lawmakers on Thursday approved a security agreement with U.S. President Donald Trump covering Greenland, seeking to end months of strained diplomatic tensions over the island's future.Trump and the prime ministers of Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September. It allows Washington to expand its military presence on the island, paving the way for two new bases and the construction of a "Golden Dome" missile defense system.Thursday's approval follows a protracted period in which Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the self-governing Danish territory. Tensions reached fever pitch in January as the president repeatedly insisted that the U.S. needed Greenland for its national security, at times declining to rule out using military force to acquire it.A parliamentary tally showed 109 Danish lawmakers unanimously backed the agreement on Thursday, per Reuters. Greenland's parliament ratified the deal earlier this month. It is not subject to a vote in the U.S. Senate.NEW YORK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 22: (L-R) U.S. President Donald Trump, Prime Minister of Denmark Mette Frederiksen and Prime Minister of Greenland Jens-Frederik Nielsen hold up the proclamations during the signing of a security pact between the U.S., Denmark, and Greenland during the 81st session of the United Nations (U.N.) General Assembly at U.N. Headquarters on September 22, 2026 in New York City.  Chip Somodevilla | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesThe Danish government can now formally notify the U.S. that both parliaments have consented to complete the ratification process.The deal supplements an existing 1951 defense agreement. It also maintains Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.Trump's proposed Golden Dome is a multibillion-dollar initiative designed to shield the U.S. from a range of aerial and missile threats. It was rolled out in May last year and is often compared with Israel's "Iron Dome" system.Trump's threats alarmed Greenlanders and other Europeans and opened a rift between the U.S. and NATO, of which Denmark and the U.S. are both members. Greenland has maintained that it is not for sale, and the European Union earlier this year united to rebuke Trump. — CNBC's Kevin Breuninger & Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Denmark ratifies Trump security deal over Greenland after months of diplomatic tensions

title: AMD dives on short-seller report of alleged China exposure
description: watch nowShares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleg
body: watch nowShares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."CNBC did not independently verify this information.Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconAMD, 1-dayThe allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia. "The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.AMD continued to slide after-hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

schema.headline: AMD dives on short-seller report of alleged China exposure

title: Novartis raises blockbuster drug forecasts to $18 billion as it seeks to prove growth can last
description: Pharma major Novartis is becoming more optimistic about some of its biggest growth drugs, even as investors question the company's ability to sustain
body: Pharma major Novartis is becoming more optimistic about some of its biggest growth drugs, even as investors question the company's ability to sustain growth beyond 2031 and offset the financial impact of older drugs' patent expiries. The Swiss drugmaker now expects multiple sclerosis drug Kesimpta, leukaemia treatment Scemblix, and cholesterol medicine Leqvio to generate $18 billion in peak sales, up from a previous forecast of $14 billion combined.CEO Vas Narasimhan said the upgrades were driven primarily by strong commercial performance, pointing to growing market share for Kesimpta and Scemblix and robust demand for Leqvio in the U.S. and Asia.Vas Narasimhan, chief executive officer of Novartis AG, during an announcement in the Roosevelt Room of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Friday, Dec. 19, 2025. Will Oliver | Bloomberg | Getty Images"It's really that in-market commercial performance that's driving these upgrades," Narasimhan told reporters on Thursday.Shares fell 2.4% in mid-morning trading in Switzerland. For investors, the question will be whether those drugs can grow fast enough to offset lost sales as other drugs face competition from cheaper rivals entering the market.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNovartis shares year-to-date.Even so, the overall growth outlook looked slightly more cautious despite stronger expectations for some key growth drugs.Novartis projected annual sales growth of 5% through 2031, slightly less ambitious than its previous guidance of between 5% and 6% through 2030, although it covers a different five-year period. CEO Vas Narasimhan said the revised outlook reflected the expected entry of U.S. generic competition for Kisqali, a breast cancer treatment, in the second half of 2031.Citi analysts noted the 2031 sales guidance was about 3% above consensus, adding they expect the market to remain skeptical of post-2031 growth, pending further pipeline data. Novartis has faced several recent clinical setbacks. In September, its closely watched cardiovascular pelacarsen trial failed to show improved cardiovascular outcomes. The following day, its del-desiran drug for muscle-wasting disorder failed in a late-stage trial, sending shares down nearly 11% in its worst single-day drop since 1987.Narasimhan defended the drugmaker's capital allocation strategy after the failure of its experimental drug del-desiran, which it acquired via a $12 billion deal for Avidity Biosciences earlier this year.Shareholders have differing views on acquisitions, with some favouring more aggressive dealmaking and others preferring a different approach, Narasimhan said. However, he said Novartis remained confident in its strategy, pointing to a 275% total shareholder return over the past decade, which he said placed the company among the sector's top performers.Tune in at 11 a.m. ET as Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan joins CNBC TV. Watch in real time on CNBC+ or the CNBC Pro stream.

schema.headline: Novartis raises blockbuster drug forecasts to $18 billion as it seeks to prove growth can last

title: Trump praises ‘great relationship’ with Putin after meeting, as Ukraine war takes center stage
description: TOPSHOT - In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump att
body: TOPSHOT - In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump attend a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 19, 2026. (Photo by Vyacheslav PROKOFYEV / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)Vyacheslav Prokofyev | Afp | Getty ImagesSHENZHEN, China — U.S. President Donald Trump met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping individually on Thursday, ahead of a scheduled trilateral with his Russian and Chinese counterparts, according to pool notes and Chinese state media.On greeting the Russian president on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, Trump said he had a "great relationship" with Putin, adding they had known each other for a long time and expressed hope that "a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."The two presidents were meeting for the first time since a summit in Alaska in August last year.Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said the talks lasted for approximately 40 minutes, and Putin left the meeting place in "an excellent mood," according to Russian state news outlet Ria Novosti.Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine was a key topic for the talks, Ushakov said, alongside preparations for the trilateral summit with China's Xi.US President Donald Trump and China's president Xi Jinping pose for a photo during a bilateral meeting in Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 19, 2026. (Photo by Doug MILLS / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)Doug Mills | Afp | Getty ImagesIn a separate bilateral meeting, Trump said he had discussed the Ukraine war with Xi, saying they should work together to bring an end to it. "We're looking to both help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine," Trump said, according to Reuters. "I'd like to see it ended," he added.Xi, meanwhile, said the two countries should cooperate to prevent artificial intelligence safety risks and strengthen communication on trade, according to Chinese state media.Earlier on Thursday, the leaders and other members of APEC gathered for a summit. Trump and Xi entered the room side by side.Xi said China would provide $20 million to support APEC cooperation, and establish a "Center for Asia-Pacific Community Studies in Shenzhen to conduct policy research and exchanges and provide intellectual support."Later in the morning session, Trump said that he opposed regulating artificial intelligence as it would "stifle" the industry. "The United States has been a Pacific power for hundreds of years, and we continue to work to promote growth and stability, sovereignty, prosperity, and peace throughout this region," Trump said.U.S. officials said last week that Trump did not plan to raise Nvidia's Jensen Huang and allegations of an affair with a Chinese spy at his meetings."By hosting APEC in Shenzhen, China took the opportunity to showcase another of its economic powerhouse cities, this time one that is home to some of the country's leading technology companies and innovators," AmCham China President Michael Hart said. "The scale of China's economic strength and technological ambition is clear to U.S. businesses," he said. "They recognize the importance of the Chinese market, but also understand that they need to remain competitive, innovative, and prepared to compete in an increasingly sophisticated business environment."

schema.headline: Trump praises ‘great relationship’ with Putin after meeting, as Ukraine war takes center stage

title: Kash Patel skips House hearing after Mar-a-Lago gala with $50,000 access
description: Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel listens as Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the
body: Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel listens as Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice building on April 21, 2026 in Washington, D.C.Anna Moneymaker | Getty ImagesAfter a string of outages disrupted airlines, banks and even the National Security Agency, U.S. House members gathered Wednesday to question the nation's top security officials. But FBI Director Kash Patel was nowhere to be seen.The night before, Patel and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had been advertised as "honored guests" at the Big Blue Bash, a lavish charitable fundraiser at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, where attendees were offered access to a "private roundtable" and a stay at the venue for $50,000 a person.Mullin appeared before lawmakers Wednesday morning at the House Homeland Security Committee's annual threat assessment hearing. Patel sent his deputy instead. And as the hearing got underway, a Justice Department jet that's been used by Patel before was still flying back from Florida.Flight records reviewed by CNBC show the Justice Department aircraft associated with Patel's travel left West Palm Beach, Florida, at 7:51 a.m. ET Wednesday and landed at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington at 10:20 a.m. ET — 20 minutes after the House Homeland Security Committee hearing began.The FBI confirmed Patel, Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche attended the Mar-a-Lago event. "The event is approved by Ethics, following all guidelines and regulations," FBI spokesperson Benjamin Williamson told CNBC by email, noting the gala "is an annual event honoring fallen law enforcement officers and their families."Patel's absence drew bipartisan criticism on Capitol Hill. Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino, R-N.Y., said lawmakers had spent months trying to secure Patel's testimony, only for the FBI director to make clear he had "no intention" of appearing.Rep. Bennie Thompson, of Mississippi, the committee's top Democrat, said Patel's absence for a second consecutive year undermined lawmakers' ability to conduct oversight. Before 2024, FBI directors traditionally testified at the annual hearing.The episode also drew attention to what was being offered at Trump's private club: a chance for donors and corporate sponsors to meet privately with some of the nation's most powerful law enforcement officials."Trump's Big Blue Bash is yet another fundraising event that encourages wealthy special interests, particularly those seeking lucrative government contracts, to rub elbows with officials responsible for awarding those contracts," Craig Holman, a government ethics and lobbying expert at the watchdog group Public Citizen, told CNBC.Billed as a tribute to federal officers and their families, the second annual black-tie gala came with a price list for access.Gala tickets cost up to $50,000General admission cost nearly $5,000, a VIP all-access pass $25,000, and a private roundtable with federal agency heads and a night at Trump's resort $50,000, according to the event's ticketing page. A sponsorship prospectus reviewed by CNBC advertised corporate packages reaching $1 million, including private briefings, speaking time, and the chance to name and present an award to a federal agency of the sponsor's choosing.Alongside Patel and Mullin, the advertised guest list also included White House border czar Tom Homan and leaders of Customs and Border Protection, the Secret Service, Drug Enforcement Administration, and Transportation Security Administration.It remains unclear which officials attended private meetings or which companies bought the most expensive packages. But several sponsors had substantial business with the agencies represented.Motorola Solutions, the gala's top named sponsor, had approximately $237.1 million in fiscal 2026 net contract obligations from the Justice and Homeland Security departments, according to CNBC's analysis of federal records. That included a $139.6 million Bureau of Prisons radio contract, a $25.8 million Customs and Border Protection award and a nearly $18 million Secret Service contract option, all in September.Motorola reported roughly $1.69 million in federal lobbying expenses this year through September, according to its first-quarter, second-quarter and third-quarter disclosures. Its lobbying included homeland security funding, communications technology and other issues."Motorola Solutions was proud to support last night's Big Blue Bash, honoring the families of wounded and fallen federal officers, whom we hosted as the night's guests of honor," the company said through a spokesperson. "We did not participate in private briefings."Federal contractors supported galaTwo other federal contractors, the Vierra Group and Teya Diversified Services, sponsored a Department of Homeland Security presentation featuring Mullin and Homan, according to the gala's published program.Federal contracting records show Teya received three Customs and Border Protection contracts in September worth approximately $23.3 million combined for repairs at northern border ports of entry. The awards were $9.1 million for work at 12 ports, $7.9 million for nine ports and $6.4 million for 10 ports.LEO Technologies, which markets artificial intelligence and surveillance products to law enforcement agencies, was also listed as a sponsor.Vierra, Teya and LEO Technologies didn't immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.Ethics rules limit charitable involvementFederal ethics rules require authorization for officials to participate in charitable fundraising in their official capacities and restrict the use of government titles for personal fundraising.Holman said companies attending such events hope to gain favor with the administration and ultimately benefit through government contracts and policies affecting their businesses.There is no evidence the sponsorships influenced federal contracts or secured preferential treatment, and some new contract awards added to existing contracts.The financial questions extend to Trump's own business. Organizers haven't disclosed what Mar-a-Lago was paid or how much reached the Federal Law Enforcement Officers Foundation, the nonprofit that's the event's beneficiary. The gala offered a $1 million sponsorship package — more than the charity's entire 2024 revenue of $725,476, according to its latest available IRS filing — though no purchase has been confirmed. A Republican fundraiser at Mar-a-Lago cost about $318,000 in 2023, according to a New York Times analysis of campaign finance records.The event also may raise questions about taxpayer-funded travel. Organizers listed Mullin as a speaker, and flight records reviewed by CNBC show a Gulfstream jet registered to DHS arriving in West Palm Beach Tuesday evening, alongside the Justice Department plane associated with Patel's travel. It remains unclear who was aboard either aircraft or whether the flights were connected to the gala.Days earlier, Mullin used a government plane to attend a Louisiana State University football game shortly after a nationwide FAA ground stop. He defended the trip Wednesday to the House Homeland Security Committee, saying that government travel was required and that he personally paid for it.

schema.headline: Kash Patel skips House hearing after Mar-a-Lago gala with $50,000 access

title: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion
description: The logo of the Italian technology company Bending Spoons SpA is pictured on the facade of the company's headquarters on November 16, 2026 in Milan, I
body: The logo of the Italian technology company Bending Spoons SpA is pictured on the facade of the company's headquarters on November 16, 2026 in Milan, Italy.Emanuele Cremaschi | Getty ImagesTax software maker Intuit said Thursday that it has agreed to sell marketing subsidiary Mailchimp to Italian technology consolidator Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion in cash and stock. The deal is set to close in early 2027, according to a statement.The sale is a costly retreat for Intuit, which paid $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021 in a push beyond its core tax and accounting businesses. Five years later, the software maker is unloading the email-marketing company for less than one-third of that price after Mailchimp became a drag on its overall revenue growth.The deal is the latest instance of Bending Spoons picking up a once promising technology asset. The company bought productivity software startup Airtable in September for 10% of what it was once worth.The Bending Spoons portfolio also contains AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo, and WeTransfer. In August Intuit started running Mailchimp as a distinct operating segment. The move was meant to give investors more transparency as the company tried to manage the unit for profitability, Sandeep Aujla, Intuit's finance chief, said at a September company briefing.Also on Thursday, Intuit announced stronger-than-expected earnings and revenue for its fiscal first quarter, which ended on Oct. 31. The company reported $2.91 in adjusted earnings per share on $4.35 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $2.70 per share and $4.31 billion in revenue. While Intuit's revenue increased 12% year over year, Mailchimp revenue declined 1% to $313 million. Analysts polled by StreetAccount had expected $314.4 million.Management called for $22.88 to $23.12 in adjusted earnings per share for the 2027 fiscal year, with $23.081 billion to $23.365 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $23.62 in adjusted earnings per share on $23.43 billion in revenue. Intuit shares tumbled 15% in extended trading.The company said Mailchimp should produce $1.256 billion to $1.266 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue, which would be down 1% to flat year over year. In August Aujla said Intuit anticipated Mailchimp's higher effective prices offsetting increased client churn. Mailchimp was founded in 2001. Rivals include Klaviyo, which went public in 2023.Berkshire Hathaway invested $600 million in Bending Spoons when the acquirer went public in July, and in October Bending Spoons said Berkshire invested another $330 million.WATCH: Intuit shares fall on guidancewatch now

schema.headline: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion

title: Takaichi gets chilly reception in China on first Japan leader visit since 2019
description: Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi walks past China's President Xi Jinping (R) after they shook hands before leaders take a group photo during the
body: Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi walks past China's President Xi Jinping (R) after they shook hands before leaders take a group photo during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 19, 2026.Greg Baker | Afp | Getty ImagesJapanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a subdued welcome on her first trip to China as premier, signaling Beijing's limited appetite for repairing ties strained by a simmering row over Taiwan.At gatherings such as this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, protocol details — including who greets a visiting leader at the airport and where they are positioned in official photographs — often convey political messages.Takaichi was met on the tarmac Wednesday by a retired Chinese diplomat, rather than a serving official, and Japan's ambassador to China, Kenji Kanasugi.The low-key reception contrasted sharply with the warmer welcomes given to other visiting leaders, including South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, while U.S. President Donald Trump was greeted personally by Chinese President Xi Jinping.In the leaders' group photo, Takaichi was placed in the back row, off to the side and several places from Xi, who stood alongside Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.U.S. President Donald Trump, front row center, speaks with Xi Jinping, China's president, front row second left, while posing for a 'family photo' with other wrold leaders during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026.Qilai Shen | Bloomberg | Getty Images"Beijing sought to downgrade her official status to that of a head of government rather than a head of state," said Jeremy Chan, senior analyst at Eurasia Group.During Thursday morning's greeting line, Takaichi spent several minutes trying to talk to the Chinese leader without an interpreter present, while most leaders exchanged handshakes and kept walking. "It has become increasingly difficult for her to engage in formal or even informal conversations with Xi," said Kei Koga, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, who sees Takaichi's intention as to still "project the image that she could still communicate with him despite the ongoing tensions."At a press briefing Thursday afternoon, Takaichi said Japan's position on Taiwan remained unchanged as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Communique, adding that her leadership has been communicating with Chinese counterparts on rare earth export controls. 'Frosty' receptionTakaichi's subdued reception signaled Beijing's lack of enthusiasm to repair ties with Tokyo, analysts said, potentially prolonging China's curbs on critical mineral exports that have gripped Japanese industries for the past year. "China's frosty reception of Takaichi shows quite clearly that Beijing is not yet ready to forgive her over her remarks about Taiwan," Chan said, expecting the bilateral relationship to remain strained until Takaichi leaves office. That could leave Japan grappling with continued restrictions on rare earth supplies from China next year, said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit. Relations deteriorated sharply after Takaichi said in November 2025 that a Taiwan Strait crisis could constitute a situation threatening Japan's survival and warrant a self-defense response. While the substance broadly aligned with Japan's existing security policy, previous prime ministers had generally avoided stating it so explicitly in a Taiwan scenario.China reacted angrily and demanded that Takaichi retract the remarks. She has not done so, while stating that the door to dialogue with Beijing remains open, with minimal high-level contact over the past year.China has since tightened restrictions affecting Japan, including controls on dual-use and rare earth exports with potential military uses. It also discouraged its citizens from traveling to Japan and halted Japanese seafood imports.watch nowTakaichi's visit marked the first trip to China by a Japanese prime minister since Shinzo Abe traveled to Chengdu in December 2019 for a trilateral summit with Chinese and South Korean leaders.No formal Takaichi-Xi meeting has been publicly scheduled during her visit. Meanwhile, Xi is expected to join Trump and Putin for a historic trilateral gathering on Thursday, alongside a bilateral meeting with Trump.Takaichi needs to show a "reflection of what she said about Taiwan a year ago," said Huiyao Wang, founder of the Beijing-based Center for China and Globalization, which is often seen as close to Beijing's thinking.  Wang said Tokyo should show greater flexibility, pointing to Trump's comments that the U.S. would avoid getting involved in the Taiwan issue. He argued that Japan holding firm on the issue would not help relations with Beijing.Such reflection, he said, "would really help to clarify some of those misunderstandings between the two countries."— CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Takaichi gets chilly reception in China on first Japan leader visit since 2019

title: Walmart hikes outlook as CEO tells CNBC retailer aims to keep prices low despite soaring fuel costs
description: watch nowWalmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce
body: watch nowWalmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season.Walmart said global e-commerce sales surged 17% in the fiscal third quarter, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter.  Walmart said it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices.CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the company has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices."The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner said in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can."CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter."This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses."Shoppers enter a Walmart store in Charlotte, North Carolina, Aug. 30, 2026.Travis Dove | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesWalmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey said Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.Walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth. Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: 65 cents adjusted vs. 64 cents expectedRevenue: $188.84 billion vs. $187.27 billion expectedFor the quarter ended Oct. 31, the company reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%.Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share.Walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.Furner also said Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average."It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he said. Sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It said its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise. In October, Walmart announced it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer stand-alone memberships, as well. Furner told CNBC the new membership has brought roughly 2 million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the company reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more."The company on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter. The company is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company said it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef.Rainey said Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start."The big-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

schema.headline: Walmart hikes outlook as CEO tells CNBC retailer aims to keep prices low despite soaring fuel costs

title: Intel signs first external customer for advanced 18A chips
description: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan speaks during a keynote presentation at Computex in Taipei on June 2, 2026. Cheng Yu-chen | AFP | Getty ImagesIntel CEO Lip-Bu Ta
body: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan speaks during a keynote presentation at Computex in Taipei on June 2, 2026. Cheng Yu-chen | AFP | Getty ImagesIntel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said on Wednesday that the company has signed the first outside customer for its 18A chips."Resilient supply on the foundry is very important," Tan said at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin, Texas. "And then 18A, I'm involved in production and we just signed the first customer," Tan added, without naming the debut client. It's a milestone moment for Intel in its five-year effort to take on chip manufacturing leader Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. After years of missteps and low yields, Intel touted 18A as key to a turnaround that would finally convert the company into a competitive chip manufacturer for non-Intel products."It's a huge win for foundry," Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin told CNBC in an interview. Pushkar Ranade, Intel's technology chief, clarified on X that the external customer had signed up for Intel's 18A-P manufacturing process node, which went into risk production in June. In May, reports indicated that Apple and Intel were closing in on a deal to use Intel's foundry to make some of the chips for Apple devices.Intel's stock has lost more than half its value since the end of September, with most of that plunge coming late last month after the company said revenue this quarter will be at least $1 billion shy of analysts' estimates due to a PC sales slump and supply chain challenges. In considering who the customer may be, Bajarin pointed to Nvidia, Apple or the major hyperscalers that make their own custom processors. "Amazon, Microsoft and Google are struggling to get capacity for their CPU ambitions at TSMC," he said. "So it makes sense that you go somewhere for at least some capacity."Tan said in late October that he sees the global market for server processors increasing as much as five times over the next five years to about $200 billion, but that Intel can't currently meet customer demand. Wall Street has turned on Intel of late after the chipmaker had become a top trade starting in the middle of last year. The U.S. government took a 10% stake in Intel in August 2025, and Nvidia followed with a $5 billion investment, as optimism grew around the prospect of U.S.-made chips that could replace an almost complete reliance on Taiwan.Until now, Intel has had no marquee customer for its foundry business, primarily manufacturing chips for its own products at its factories, including a huge new campus in Arizona.Intel is a leader in another step of the chipmaking process known as advanced packaging, where individual chips are packaged together and connected to the larger system. Tan also announced on Wednesday that Microsoft is its first publicly named customer for its most advanced packaging technology, known as EMIB. —CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed to this report.WATCH: Can Intel's New Arizona Chip Fab Bring It Back From The Brink?watch now

schema.headline: Intel signs first external customer for advanced 18A chips

title: Jensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloons
description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum at the Kennedy Center in Washington, Nov. 19, 2025.Stefani Reynolds | Bloomberg | Getty
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum at the Kennedy Center in Washington, Nov. 19, 2025.Stefani Reynolds | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe still-unraveling scandal of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affairs and the tech giant's potential role in its advanced semiconductor chips ending up in China present a legal minefield for Huang and Nvidia.Federal and state prosecutors and Nvidia employees may target Huang and the company in court, where some shareholders have already taken action.That's on top of a rapidly growing pile of probes by Republicans who control Congress now and Democrats who will have majorities in both the House and Senate come January."It's not going to get any better for Jensen Huang; it's going to get far worse," said Salvatore Graziano, a New York securities litigation attorney at Bernstein, Litowitz, Berger & Grossmann. His firm is looking at shareholder lawsuit opportunities against Nvidia and Huang.[Huang] "faces the Department of Justice, the Securities and Exchange Commission and private litigation," Graziano said. "The criminal exposure is very serious. The SEC could bar him from being an officer. And the potential liability [from shareholder] lawsuits can be very large."Huang's and Nvidia's legal exposure stems from three issues that led up to his shock resignation Nov. 12.There's his alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who worked for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under investigation for diverting advanced Nvidia semiconductor chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules. That, in turn, has raised questions about whether Huang and Nvidia were aware of any diversions.There are Huang's two other alleged affairs with Nvidia employees.And there is the sharp drop in the company's stock price in the wake of the scandal. Nvidia's share price has fallen 19% since Nov. 8, when Huang sent a company-wide apology acknowledging extramarital affairs.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia share priceHuang last week retained the law firm Paul, Weiss and its attorneys Melinda Haag and Walter Brown to represent him. Haag is a former U.S. attorney in San Francisco, and Brown is also a former federal prosecutor.Huang's spokesman at Trident, a crisis communications firm, declined to comment when asked if Haag and Brown are representing him in any potential criminal case and other questions about his legal exposure.Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Last week, Nvidia retained the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation into Huang allegedly being targeted by a spy, as U.S. intelligence reportedly has concluded.Read more CNBC news on NvidiaJensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloonsTrump bought Nvidia, Palantir, SpaceX amid federal contractsKress tells employees 'let's move forward' at first all-hands meeting since Huang exitPRO: Here's what every major Wall Street analyst is saying about Nvidia after its earnings reportKress tells Jim Cramer that 'customers continue to be with us'Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China access: SourcesThe civil liability Huang and Nvidia could face is underscored by a hearing Graziano, the securities attorney, attended Tuesday in U.S. District Court in San Francisco. A judge at the hearing approved a $175 million settlement from Seagate Technology Holdings to resolve a shareholder lawsuit alleging it concealed sales of hard-disk drives to Huawei in China in violation of export bans. The Seagate settlement came three years after the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security — which is investigating Megaspeed's business with Nvidia — imposed a $300 million penalty on Seagate for its sales to Huawei.Graziano said his law firm is "actively looking at securities law liability for Nvidia, Jensen Huang and other senior executives in the company given all the recent developments regarding their [potential] knowledge and facilitation of illegal chip sales to Chinese entities." One shareholder suit has been filedThere is already a pending class-action shareholder lawsuit in San Francisco federal court against Nvidia and Huang by the Rosen Law Firm, for allegedly misleading and false statements related to Megaspeed and Alice Huang. "Several hundreds of investors have contacted us and expressed an interest to join the case — investors of all walks of life, from mom and pops to investors with very large losses," Rosen attorney Phil Kim told CNBC in an email. Katie Sweeten, a former federal prosecutor in the DOJ's National Security Division, said the question of "who knew what and when, and what was [Huang's] role" is potentially the biggest risk for Nvidia and him."Now DOJ can leverage their criminal authorities," Sweeten, a partner at Scale LLP, told CNBC's Kelly Evans on "The Exchange.""They can bring grand jury subpoenas, search warrants for emails, bank accounts, personal devices, computers, things like that," Sweeten said.While it is "not illegal to, you know, sleep with a spy ... it is illegal to pass certain types of information to a counterintelligence officer," she said.Sweeten also pointed to potential export control violations, which "could be very serious."She noted the DOJ can indict a company as well as its officials if there is evidence of criminality. Export control violations carry a maximum possible criminal sentence of 20 years in prison and "really large fines," she said."You can't send the company to prison, but they can face fines, civil penalties, debarment — where you can't export items down the line," she said.One example of that came in July 2025, when the DOJ obtained a guilty plea and an agreement to pay more than $140 million from Cadence Design Systems for violating the Export Control Reform Act by unlawfully exporting semiconductor design tools to China's National University of Defense Technology, a school led by China's Central Military Commission.Congressional hearings present riskAnother potential legal risk for Huang comes from his planned appearances before Congress.Huang is scheduled to give a closed-door interview Dec. 1 to three House committees. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., wants Huang's testimony before that panel to be public, and told CNBC Tuesday he hopes to have that happen "before Christmas."Sweeten said Huang "has to be very careful" about what he says there because of the risk of being criminally charged with lying to Congress, and of saying something "that absolutely can become part of a criminal or civil investigation.""I expect Huang to take the Fifth on most questions" from Congress, Jonathan Kanter, a former assistant attorney general in the DOJ's Antitrust Division, told CNBC, meaning Huang will likely use his constitutional right against giving testimony that could be used against him in a criminal case."With a Justice Department criminal investigation into Megaspeed already underway and more investigations possible, anything he tells Congress could be used against him," Kanter said. "His lawyers are likely to advise him against taking that risk."Ben Heineman Jr., a former senior vice president and general counsel of General Electric, and a senior fellow at Harvard University, told CNBC that Nvidia's board will be scrutinized over its actions before it pushed Huang to resign.Heineman cited the board's apparent lack of succession planning and what looks like weak oversight of Huang, including relating to personal conduct such as the two alleged affairs with Nvidia employees and with an executive of an Nvidia customer."When there is a sort of reasonable suspicion, they need to investigate it, and they don't appear to have done that," Heineman said.State attorneys general may circleNvidia and Huang could face investigation from state attorneys general, including in California, where the company is headquartered.On Tuesday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta told Bloomberg Television that the situation at Nvidia with Huang is "something that we're interested in." Bonta's office later told CNBC, "We are monitoring the situation."Huang's alleged affairs with Nvidia employees also open the possibility of workplace litigation.Ari Wilkenfeld, a Washington-area employment lawyer, said a consensual relationship between a chief executive and a subordinate "is not in and of itself illegal.""The liability never comes from the existence of the relationship alone. It comes from whether it was genuinely welcome, what job benefits flowed from it, and what it did to everyone else in the building," Wilkenfeld said. "California law recognizes that so-called sexual favoritism can create a hostile environment for an entire workforce."The affair is Huang's problem," Wilkenfeld said. "What, if anything, Nvidia did once it knew is the company's problem."

schema.headline: Jensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloons

title: Ford starts U.S. battery cell production using Chinese tech amid geopolitical tensions
description: An employee does final inspection before cells are put in shipping containers to be moved to Ford's battery pack plant that's connected to the cell ma
body: An employee does final inspection before cells are put in shipping containers to be moved to Ford's battery pack plant that's connected to the cell manufacturing facility.Courtesy FordMARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors. The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible."If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells."The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. US President Donald Trump (L) shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province on November 18, 2026.Lori Sagisawa | AFP | Getty ImagesIn September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production. Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.watch nowFord has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed. The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

schema.headline: Ford starts U.S. battery cell production using Chinese tech amid geopolitical tensions

title: Musk accuses Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield restrictions in Ukraine
description: (L-R) Andrew Ross Sorkin and Elon Musk speak during the NY Times Dealbook Summit at Jazz at Lincoln Center, Nov. 18, 2026 in New York City. Adam Gray
body: (L-R) Andrew Ross Sorkin and Elon Musk speak during the NY Times Dealbook Summit at Jazz at Lincoln Center, Nov. 18, 2026 in New York City. Adam Gray | Getty ImagesSpaceX founder Elon Musk accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being untruthful about restrictions around Ukraine's Starshield network and said Kyiv wanted to use Starlink for offensive operations.Asked at The New York Times' Dealbook Summit about Zelenskyy's claims that Starshield had been slowed down, Musk said, "That's false ... I don't want to blow your mind, but Zelenskyy is not always truthful."watch nowWhen pressed on whether he meant Ukraine was not always truthful, Musk doubled down with a reply: "No, it's not always truthful."His comments came after Zelenskyy on Wednesday said speed restrictions remained in place on Starshield, hampering Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missile and drone strikes. "We are discussing this with the American side," he said.Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, stoking a conflict that has resulted in a refugee crisis and hundreds of thousands of deaths. Ukraine has been able to beat back Russian forces more effectively than many observers thought possible, despite having a much smaller land area and population.However, it relies heavily on SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield for capabilities like battlefield communications and drone operations. Musk has previously said that "if we were to turn off Starlink, the entire Ukrainian front would collapse immediately."The SpaceX CEO sought to distinguish between Starlink, a commercial satellite network, and Starshield, a military system developed by SpaceX and operated by the U.S. government.Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.Elon MuskCEO, SpaceXMusk said that Starlink is subject to speed limits because it is not intended for offensive military operations, adding that such missions should instead use the Starshield network."Any action taken by Starshield is up to the War Department. Starlink is commercial and is not intended as a weapon of war," Musk said, referring to the U.S. Department of Defense.In October, Musk said the U.S. government and President Donald Trump were responsible for any restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield network after slowdowns to the service were reported."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote on X. The Wall Street Journal later reported on Oct. 20 that Musk had ordered the slowdown, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter."What I'm trying to tell you is Zelenskyy is actually asking to use the Starlink commercial satellites for events of military actions, and we have declined to do so, as we have declined to do so from the beginning of this conflict," Musk added in the interview.On Oct. 24, Musk said SpaceX had restricted Ukraine's access to Starlink because Kyiv had violated the service's terms by using it for offensive drone strikes, a claim Ukrainian officials disputed."Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," Musk wrote on X one day after.CNBC has reached out to Ukraine's ministry of foreign affairs for comment but did not receive a response. The president's office could not immediately be reached.

schema.headline: Musk accuses Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield restrictions in Ukraine
